title: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition) · Units 11–12
description: Nuanced language for romantic and platonic relationships, close friendships, loyalty, trust, interpersonal conflict and relationship breakdowns.
sourceNotice: Prepared for personal study with vocabulary and usage targets selected from the user-provided source. Portuguese translations, English examples and study notes are original; textbook exercise questions and longer passages are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Teaching sections A–D and A–C, all facing exercises 11.1–11.5 and 12.1–12.6, and corresponding answer-key material (including adjective/noun forms and tested prepositions).
audit.pronunciation: Broad British IPA is included only where reliable for short lexical targets; multiword items generally leave IPA blank instead of inventing full connected-speech transcriptions.
audit.languagePolicy: All learner-facing content and metadata are English except for Brazilian Portuguese in pt fields.
audit.reviewMethod: Compared vocabulary against PDF teaching pages, facing exercises and answer key; checked idioms, connotation, morphology, prepositions and source provenance. Wrote original examples and performed JSON/schema/ID and static Word-audio target lint. Browser importer and TTS playback were not tested.
audit.limitations: No recorded MP3 is included; browser import, actual speech synthesis and recognition have not been verified. Certain idioms are informal or comparatively dated, and broken home can be stigmatising; this is indicated in the cards.

units.title: Unit 11 — Relationships: friends forever
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition); printed pages 28–29 (PDF pages 30–31).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition)
units.category: People and relationships · love, friendship, affinity and positive social bonds
learningObjectives: Identify nuanced romantic and platonic expressions, including infatuated, besotted and love at first sight.
Use idioms for immediate rapport, deep friendship and strong family relationships.
Distinguish key adjective–noun families and employ their usual prepositions accurately.
Differentiate trusting from trustworthy and faith from faithfulness.

sectionsChecked: B · Friendships and other positive relationships

items.example: Their friendship developed slowly; it certainly was not love at first sight.
items.note: An instant romantic attraction when people first meet.

items.word: fall head over heels in love
items.example: After several weeks abroad, they had fallen head over heels in love.
items.note: Intensifies falling in love; head over heels is a fixed expression.

items.example: Even at a crowded reception, he only had eyes for his partner.
items.note: Means being romantically interested in one person alone; fixed figurative expression.

items.pt: estar apaixonado de maneira intensa ou idealizada por alguém
items.example: She was infatuated with the musician without knowing him personally.
items.note: Infatuation can imply a strong but unreasoning or short-lived attraction; use with.

items.pt: estar perdidamente apaixonado ou encantado por alguém
items.example: He was so besotted with her that he overlooked the warning signs.
items.note: An intense, almost uncritical affection; stronger than being merely fond of someone.

items.pt: relacionamento platônico; vínculo afetivo sem envolvimento sexual
items.example: They maintained a close but purely platonic relationship for decades.
items.note: Platonic describes affection or closeness without sexual involvement; it is not necessarily romantic.

items.example: Both friends insisted their relationship was platonic.
items.note: Frequently used with friendship, relationship and love.

items.pt: se dar bem logo de cara; criar afinidade imediata
items.example: The two researchers hit it off at their first conference.
items.note: Informal phrasal idiom for becoming friendly immediately; often hit it off with someone.

items.pt: alma gêmea; pessoa com quem se tem profunda afinidade
items.example: For her, a soulmate was someone who understood her values and fears.
items.note: Not restricted to romantic partners; also possible for very close friends.

items.word: a person after my own heart
items.pt: pessoa que pensa ou age como eu; alguém de quem gosto por afinidade
items.example: Anyone who brings homemade food to a meeting is a person after my own heart.
items.note: Approving idiom for someone whose tastes or attitudes are similar to yours; after my own heart is fixed.

items.word: get on like a house on fire
items.pt: dar-se extraordinariamente bem; ter ótima sintonia
items.example: The new flatmates got on like a house on fire from day one.
items.note: British informal expression for having an exceptionally friendly relationship.

items.example: The two artists remained bosom friends throughout their careers.
items.note: Very close friends; bosom can sound literary or old-fashioned in this expression.

items.example: Although they argued, they had been bosom pals since childhood.
items.note: Informal phrase used by the book; less common in everyday speech than close friends.

items.example: The neighbours became bosom buddies after working on the community garden.
items.note: Informal, sometimes humorous term for exceptionally close friends.

items.example: The sisters were inseparable throughout their school years.
items.note: Describes people who spend most of their time together.

items.example: Years of collaboration created a close bond among the volunteers.
items.note: Bond refers to emotional connectedness and can link friends, relatives or colleagues.

items.pt: almas afins; pessoas com grande afinidade
items.example: The two writers were kindred spirits despite their different backgrounds.
items.note: People who share attitudes, ideas or feelings; often plural.

items.pt: casal muito compatível; casal que combina bem
items.example: Their shared priorities make them a well-matched couple.
items.note: Well-matched describes compatible partners; it does not mean that their appearances are identical.

items.example: Strong family ties influenced her decision to remain in the city.
items.note: Fixed collocation for relationships and obligations among relatives.

items.example: We discovered several mutual acquaintances at the alumni dinner.
items.note: Acquaintances are people you know but are not necessarily close friends.

items.pt: ter alguém em alta consideração; respeitar muito alguém
items.example: The trainees held their supervisor in high regard.
items.note: A relatively formal expression for strong respect or admiration; also hold someone in great regard.

items.pt: unidos como unha e carne; muito chegados
items.example: Those cousins are as thick as thieves and rarely go anywhere separately.
items.note: Informal simile for two people who are very close and may share secrets; does not imply actual theft.

items.pt: adorador; cheio de carinho e admiração
items.example: An adoring crowd waited patiently to greet the singer.
items.note: Often suggests strong affectionate admiration; adoration is the noun.

items.example: The child looked at her grandmother with open adoration.
items.note: A noun expressing intense affection or admiration, often tender.

items.example: His affectionate farewell reassured the entire family.
items.note: Used of warm, loving behaviour; typically affectionate towards someone.

items.example: She expressed affection through small acts of kindness.
items.note: The noun for warm liking and care; not necessarily romantic.

items.example: The amiable host made every guest feel welcome.
items.note: Describes pleasant friendliness or a good-natured temperament.

items.example: Her amiability helped calm an otherwise tense discussion.
items.note: Relatively formal noun corresponding to amiable.

items.pt: atencioso; que leva os outros em consideração
items.example: It was considerate of him to warn his neighbours about the noise.
items.note: A considerate person thinks about other people’s needs and feelings.

items.pt: consideração; atenção aos sentimentos e necessidades alheios
items.example: Please show some consideration for people working nearby.
items.note: Here the noun concerns thoughtfulness, not merely careful deliberation.

items.example: They remained faithful to each other despite a long separation.
items.note: Describes loyalty to a partner or cause; the related noun is faithfulness.

items.example: Mutual faithfulness was essential to their relationship.
items.note: Loyal commitment to someone; distinct from faith meaning trust or belief.

items.pt: afeiçoado; que gosta muito de alguém
items.example: I am fond of my former colleagues and still visit them.
items.note: Usually followed by of, not for; may describe affection without romance.

items.example: He developed a fondness for quiet seaside towns.
items.note: Often fondness for someone or something; can express personal liking.

items.example: She remained loyal to the team during a difficult season.
items.note: Loyal to someone or something; fidelity and dependability are central.

items.example: Her loyalty to her colleagues was never in doubt.
items.note: The noun paired with loyal; may involve personal or professional allegiance.

items.example: Their passion gradually became a calmer kind of affection.
items.note: Can refer to intense romantic feeling or strong enthusiasm for an activity.

items.example: They were still passionate about each other after many years.
items.note: The related adjective is passionate; often passionate about someone or something.

items.example: What began as a friendship slowly developed into a romance.
items.note: Noun for a romantic relationship; romantic is the related adjective.

items.example: The evening felt romantic without being extravagant.
items.note: Describes romantic feelings, relationships or gestures.

items.example: His devotion to his ageing parents was evident in everything he did.
items.note: The noun of devoted; can be religious, familial or personal.

items.example: She was devoted to her younger brother.
items.note: Typically devoted to someone or something, never devoted with.

items.example: The mentoring programme offered emotional and practical support.
items.note: Here a noun; the adjective supportive describes someone who gives such help.

items.example: A supportive colleague helped her through the transition.
items.note: Commonly supportive of someone or something.

items.example: It took time to rebuild their trust after the misunderstanding.
items.note: The noun trust is normally uncountable in this sense; related to trusting and trustworthy.

items.pt: confiante; que confia facilmente nos outros
items.example: A trusting child may not recognise when someone is being dishonest.
items.note: A trusting person is willing to trust others; not the same as trustworthy.

items.example: The committee needed a trustworthy person to handle the donations.
items.note: Other people can safely trust a trustworthy person; distinct from trusting.

items.example: She had enormous respect for her former lecturer.
items.note: Use respect for someone in this noun construction.

items.example: Students are expected to be respectful towards their peers.
items.note: Usually respectful of or respectful towards someone or something.

items.pt: paixão intensa e idealizada; encantamento exagerado
items.example: His infatuation faded once they got to know each other.
items.note: The noun of infatuated; implies an intense attraction that may be unrealistic.

items.example: Despite living abroad, he remained devoted to his family.
items.note: The required preposition is to.

items.example: I have great respect for researchers who share their methods openly.
items.note: Noun respect takes for in this construction.

items.example: She stayed loyal to her friends through the dispute.
items.note: The correct preposition after loyal is to.

items.pt: dar apoio a alguém; apoiar alguém
items.example: The department was supportive of staff pursuing further training.
items.note: In this construction supportive takes of.

items.pt: ter carinho por alguém; gostar muito de alguém
items.example: I am fond of my neighbours but prefer to live alone.
items.note: Fond takes of, and it does not necessarily indicate romantic love.

items.example: The director put considerable trust in the new team.
items.note: Use put trust in; compare have trust in.

items.example: She was affectionate towards the children in her care.
items.note: A frequent adjective–preposition pattern in this context is affectionate towards.

items.example: They were just as passionate about each other as they had been before.
items.note: The book tests passionate about in a relationship context; passionate about also works for interests.

units.title: Unit 12 — Relationships: ups and downs
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition); printed pages 30–31 (PDF pages 32–33).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition)
units.category: People and relationships · loyalty, conflict and relationship breakdowns
learningObjectives: Distinguish casual acquaintances, friends, colleagues, allies, partners and rivals.
Express disapproval and loyalty with accurate modifiers and prepositions.
Describe breakdowns, long-running disagreements and unstable relationships with idiomatic language.
Recognise register and social sensitivity when discussing strained family relationships.

items.example: He had several casual acquaintances in the new neighbourhood but no close friends.
items.note: An acquaintance is someone you know but are not necessarily close to; casual makes the distance explicit.

items.example: A true friend will be honest even when the truth is uncomfortable.
items.note: A stronger bond than that of a casual acquaintance.

items.pt: estar presente quando alguém precisa; dar apoio
items.example: She was there for me when I lost my job.
items.note: Informal supportive expression; it means being dependable, not merely physically present.

items.example: I avoid speaking ill of colleagues who are not in the room.
items.note: Speak ill of is a relatively formal expression meaning criticise or say negative things about.

items.example: They criticised the policy behind their manager’s back.
items.note: Means without the person knowing, often suggesting disloyalty or secrecy.

items.example: A colleague offered to cover her shift during the emergency.
items.note: A person you work with; not necessarily a friend.

items.pt: aliado; pessoa ou grupo que apoia uma causa
items.example: The campaign found an unexpected ally among local businesses.
items.note: An ally may cooperate toward a shared goal without being a close friend.

items.example: She asked her business partner to review the contract.
items.note: Can refer to a romantic partner, a business associate or a collaborator depending on context.

items.example: They regarded his secret deal with a competitor as disloyal.
items.note: The opposite of loyal; typically disloyal to someone.

items.example: The group interpreted the leaked information as an act of disloyalty.
items.note: Noun derived from disloyal; usually uncountable in the general sense.

items.pt: que não dá apoio; pouco solidário
items.example: An unsupportive supervisor can make a difficult project even harder.
items.note: Opposite of supportive; describes a lack of needed encouragement or assistance.

items.pt: crítico; que desaprova ou aponta defeitos
items.example: He became increasingly critical of the proposed changes.
items.note: In relationships, critical of often means disapproving; can also mean important or analytical elsewhere.

items.example: Please be honest about the difficulties you encountered.
items.note: Means not deceptive; compare truthful, which stresses telling the truth.

items.example: The witness gave a truthful account of the incident.
items.note: Emphasises communicating what is true; typically truthful about something.

items.example: The audit exposed a dishonest attempt to conceal expenses.
items.note: Opposite of honest; dishonest with someone in interpersonal contexts.

items.pt: que mente; que não diz a verdade
items.example: The article was untruthful about the organisation’s finances.
items.note: Opposite of truthful; specifically suggests a failure to tell the truth.

items.example: It was disrespectful to interrupt the speaker repeatedly.
items.note: Opposite of respectful; often disrespectful towards someone.

items.example: Her remarks showed disrespect for the people who had volunteered.
items.note: Noun for lack of respect; also a verb in some contexts.

items.pt: falso; dissimulado; que age de modo diferente pelas costas
items.example: She seemed friendly in person but was two-faced when discussing her colleagues.
items.note: Disapproving of someone who is pleasant face to face but behaves differently behind your back.

items.example: The two business partners agreed to share responsibility for the new venture.
items.note: Partners jointly own or operate a business; rivals compete with one another.

items.pt: rivais ferrenhos; adversários com forte animosidade
items.example: The former collaborators became bitter rivals after the dispute.
items.note: Bitter intensifies hostility; not all competitors are bitter rivals.

items.example: The clubs are arch rivals despite competing in different leagues.
items.note: Arch- marks an especially prominent, long-standing rivalry.

items.example: Once close allies, the two politicians became sworn enemies.
items.note: Very strong expression for persistent hatred or hostility.

items.pt: ser frio ou distante com alguém
items.example: Since the disagreement, he has been distant towards his sister.
items.note: Here distant means emotionally cold, not physically far away.

items.example: The treasurer was scrupulously honest about every expense.
items.note: Scrupulously intensifies honest and stresses careful integrity.

items.example: The organisation demanded complete loyalty from its members.
items.note: Complete is an intensifier; demanding absolute loyalty may be context-dependent.

items.example: His unswerving loyalty to the team earned widespread respect.
items.note: Unswerving means unwavering or not changing, especially of commitment or loyalty.

items.example: The scientist gained a staunch ally in the university president.
items.note: Staunch suggests very loyal and reliable support; often political or professional.

items.example: The reviewers were deeply critical of the decision to exclude participants.
items.note: Deeply can intensify disapproval; the usual preposition after critical is of.

items.pt: um relacionamento se desfaz; uma relação entra em colapso
items.example: Their working relationship broke down after repeated disputes.
items.note: Break down means stop functioning successfully; used for personal and institutional relationships.

items.example: It was a genuine misunderstanding rather than a deliberate insult.
items.note: Genuine contrasts with a deliberate or fabricated excuse.

items.pt: surge uma ruptura entre pessoas; abre-se um afastamento grave
items.example: A rift developed between the siblings over the inheritance.
items.note: Rift is a serious disagreement that damages relationships, not just a minor argument.

items.example: Disagreements about priorities created discord within the committee.
items.note: Somewhat formal noun for conflict or lack of harmony in a group.

items.pt: não concordar; não ter a mesma opinião
items.example: My supervisor and I do not see eye to eye on remote working.
items.note: Idiomatic expression of disagreement; often not see eye to eye on something.

items.word: be on bad terms with someone
items.pt: estar de relações cortadas ou ruins com alguém
items.example: She has been on bad terms with her neighbour since the dispute.
items.note: Fixed expression describing a poor relationship; contrasting form is on good terms.

items.pt: azedar; deteriorar-se (sobre uma relação ou situação)
items.example: What began as a promising collaboration gradually turned sour.
items.note: Figurative meaning: become unpleasant or unfriendly; not about food here.

items.example: They decided to split up amicably after many years together.
items.note: Informal phrasal verb for ending a romantic relationship; can also mean divide a group.

items.example: Their marriage has had its ups and downs, but they remain committed.
items.note: A fixed idiom for alternating good and difficult periods.

items.pt: relacionamento conturbado; relação com altos e baixos
items.example: It was a bumpy relationship marked by frequent arguments.
items.note: Bumpy is figurative for unstable, with recurring difficulties.

items.pt: família desfeita por separação dos pais; lar de pais separados
items.example: She disliked being labelled as coming from a broken home.
items.note: Traditional term for a family disrupted by separation or divorce; can sound judgemental or dated.

items.pt: briga familiar duradoura; desavença de família
items.example: The family feud continued for years after the property dispute.
items.note: A long-running bitter conflict among relatives; feud is pronounced /fjuːd/.

items.example: The feud between the two families lasted for generations.
items.note: A serious and lasting conflict, usually involving people or groups.

items.example: He admitted he had been dishonest with his business partner.
items.note: The book tests dishonest with someone, not dishonest to someone.

items.pt: ser crítico em relação a alguém
items.example: The director was critical of employees who ignored safety rules.
items.note: Use critical of rather than critical with for disapproval.

items.example: She felt he had been disloyal to the team by revealing private plans.
items.note: Use disloyal to someone in this pattern.

items.example: It damages trust when team members talk behind each other’s backs.
items.note: Behind someone’s back describes concealed discussion about them, usually negative.

items.pt: ser falso ou dissimulado com alguém
items.example: He was two-faced towards his manager, praising him openly but mocking him privately.
items.note: The exercise tests two-faced towards someone; it implies insincerity.

items.word: be on good terms with someone
items.example: Despite competing for grants, the departments remained on good terms.
items.note: Positive counterpart of be on bad terms with someone, added as a useful contrast.

items.example: She remained friendly despite their disagreement.
items.note: The exercise contrasts friendly with emotionally distant.
